Headline: Tata-Adani's entry into Missile Manufacturing! What is the Modi government's plan? Astra Missile | Defence
Summary:
- Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government plans to invite private firms like Tata and Adani to manufacture missiles.
- This move aims to boost India's defense production, reduce dependency, and transform the nation into a major global weapons exporter.
- Collaborations between private companies and the Defense Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) are expected to accelerate technological growth and strengthen national security.
Translation unavailable: India no longer wants to be just a country that buys weapons, but wants to become a power that sells weapons to the world. In this direction, the Modi government is preparing to take a big step. There is news that the Indian government is seriously considering the entry of private companies into the sensitive defense sector like missile manufacturing. That is, in the coming time, Tata, Adani, Mahindra, Bharat Forge and many big Indian companies will not remain limited to vehicles, infrastructure or telecom, but can also make missiles. But the question is, why is the government feeling the need to do this? Are government companies not able to meet the demand for missiles? And if private companies enter the defense sector, what will India benefit from this? Let's understand in detail. Hello, my name is Tanmay and you are watching 'Nau Bharat Life'. Actually, in the last few years, India has taken steps towards self-reliance in the defense sector rapidly. In such a situation, the government's goal is that India can be included among the big defense exporters of the world. This is the reason why special focus is being given to defense production under the 'Make in India' and 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' campaigns. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's recent visit to Indonesia has also created a new opportunity. Indonesia has shown interest in India's indigenous air-to-air missile 'Astra Mark-2'. This is not an ordinary missile; the Astra missile has been developed by the DRDO, that is, the Defence Research and Development Organisation. This is a Beyond Visual Range, or BVR, missile. This means it can target an enemy aircraft from such a distance that the pilot cannot even see it with his own eyes. The strike capability of the Astra Mark-2 is said to be about 180 to 200 kilometers. It can track and destroy enemy aircraft that change direction at high speed. This is the reason why many countries of the world are eyeing this missile today. But here, another big challenge is coming to the fore. Currently, the production of Astra missile is mainly done by the government company 'Bharat Dynamics Limited' or BDL. The problem is that the current production capacity is not able to meet the requirements of the Indian Army and Air Force. In such a situation, if big orders start coming from abroad, it will become necessary to increase production. This is where the role of private companies begins. According to sources, the government is now planning to include big private players in defense production. In this list, the names of Tata Group, Adani Group, Mahindra, Bharat Forge, IComm, and several other companies are coming up. These companies already have experience in heavy engineering, manufacturing, electronics, and high-tech production. The government believes that if the capacity of these companies is utilized in the defense sector, the pace of missile production can increase manifold. In fact, after Operation 'Sindoor', the world's perception of Indian weapons has suddenly changed. During this operation, there were discussions at the international level about Indian defense technology and the capability of indigenous weapons. The BrahMos missile has already made its mark in the world. Countries like the Philippines have already purchased BrahMos, and now the Astra missile is also becoming a subject of discussion in the international market. This means India has a big opportunity. If production is increased, India can take a big leap in the field of defense exports. The government believes that the participation of private companies in the defense sector will not only increase production but also increase competition, new technology will come, R&D will gain momentum, and new employment opportunities will be created. However, the defense sector is not a normal industry. It is a matter related to national security, so the government will not allow any private company to make missiles directly. Strict security standards, technical qualifications, and government surveillance will be in place for this. It is likely that in the beginning, private companies will work with government agencies and DRDO to produce, meaning the technology will be the government's and the private sector will cooperate in production. This model is already being used in many countries of the world. In countries like America, France, Britain, and Israel, a large part of defense production is in the hands of private companies. India is also now seen moving in that direction. Experts believe that if this plan is successful, India will not only fulfill the needs of its army but will also be able to record a strong presence in the global defense market. The demand for weapons is increasing rapidly across the world. Amid the Ukraine war, tension in West Asia, and the security challenges in the Indo-Pacific region, many countries want to increase their military strength. In such a situation, this can become a big economic and strategic opportunity for India. That is, in the coming time, companies like Tata, Adani, and Mahindra can play an important role not only in the business world but also in strengthening India's defense technology. And if that happens, India's defense sector can enter a new era, where India will not just buy weapons, but will move forward in the direction of becoming a superpower that sells weapons to the world. It remains to be seen when and in what form the government implements this plan. But it is certain that a big change has knocked in India's defense sector. What is your opinion about this news? Please tell us by commenting.

Headline: Have the Three Armed Forces Snubbed Rajnath Singh? A Rebellion Over Agniveer!
Summary: In 2022, the Modi government launched the Agnipath (Agniveer) scheme as a major reform for the armed forces, but it faced immediate opposition from Rahul Gandhi, other politicians, and ex-military personnel who advocated for a permanent army, warning of harm to national security and military ethos. The government, however, proceeded with the scheme. Now, all three branches of the armed forces – Army, Navy, and Air Force – are collectively demanding that the Agniveer system be discontinued, specifically challenging the provision of retaining only 25% of Agniveers after four years of service. They propose increasing this retention to at least 50%, with the Navy aiming for 75%, arguing that four years is insufficient to train expert soldiers, especially in technical fields. The current system leads to poor returns on training investment as 75% of trained personnel leave. Lessons from Operation Sindoor highlighted the need for experienced personnel and to address a shortage of 1.8 lakh soldiers. The government's reluctance stems from a desire to avoid pension costs, prioritizing weapon procurement over soldier benefits. The proposal is currently under discussion in the Ministry of Defence, and the government is now considering welfare measures for martyred or disabled Agniveers, echoing earlier opposition concerns. The armed forces assert that national defense cannot be compromised and a permanent, highly trained force is essential.
Translation unavailable: In 2022, the government, the Modi government, launched a very major scheme called Agniveer. It was stated to be a huge reform in the army. The opposition and Rahul Gandhi opposed it, saying, 'Withdraw it, the country needs a permanent army, not a contractual one.' Many former military personnel also opposed it, stating that it would hurt the fundamental spirit of the army and harm the nation. But the government said, 'Modi ji does things after careful consideration.' Its implementation began in 2022. The government did not listen to the opposition, experts, or ex-army personnel. Now, the army itself has bluntly told the government: 'We don't want more Agniveers; this Agniveer system will not work anymore.' The Air Force, Navy, and Army are all saying, 'End this four-year system, it cannot continue now.' Under the Agniveer scheme, only 25% of Agniveers who completed four years of service would get permanent jobs. Now, the Army, Navy, and Air Force are collectively saying in one voice that this 25% system will not work; increase it. 'Let the army work as an army should. This contractual-based army system cannot work in India. Increase the 25%.' According to an Indian Express report, the difficulties faced by the army during Operation Sindoor last year made them realize that Agniveer sounds good, it might be Modi ji's dream, but it's not right for the army. All three armed forces want this 25% to be increased. The Navy wants it to be 75%, while the Army and Air Force want a target of at least 50%. This is a bone of contention for the government because they don't want to pay pensions. They say they have money to buy weapons but not to give pensions to soldiers. This proposal has not been finalized yet; discussions are ongoing in the Ministry of Defence. The three armed forces want to increase it because you cannot make any soldier an expert in four years. In many technical jobs in the Navy, it takes more than three years just to learn basic operations. If 75% of trained soldiers leave, the return on training investment is low. The army needs soldiers for a longer duration after their training. The lesson from Operation Sindoor is that Agniveers should be given more time so that they become experienced. The 25% limit must be removed. There is also a shortage of soldiers, approximately 1.8 lakh soldiers are needed. This will only happen when the 25% clause is removed. Besides increasing retention, the government might consider lifelong financial assistance for the families of martyred Agniveers, free treatment for disabled Agniveers, and medical cover. This means the government is now willing to accept many of the objections raised by Rahul Gandhi, which it previously rejected, because the army is saying in unison: 'We don't want Agniveers; we want more permanent, trained army personnel.' They should be vigilant and be able to capture their enemy in the blink of an eye. It should not be that someone we trained for four years retired after four years. That means the number of retirees will be high, and trained people will keep retiring. New people will come, they will also be trained, and they will retire. Who will you get work from? When the training period itself is so long. When technology is advanced and there is no shortcut to understanding that technology, you have to give it time. Now the government is realizing, perhaps it will understand, because the file is still pending in the Ministry of Defence, what the army wants. What is the need of this country? The army is saying that compromise with the country's defense and security will not work anymore.

Headline: Op Sindoor transformation of Indian Military continues
Summary: The Ministry of Defence, through the Defence Acquisition Council chaired by Rajnath Singh, approved several key military upgrades. Other significant approvals are jet-based Kamikaze drones for self-destructing attacks, a medium-range surface-to-air missile system, the VSHORADS for very short-range missile defense, and enhanced armor protection for tanks. These decisions aim to transform and strengthen India's military, incorporating lessons learned from past operations and the 2020-2024 stand-off with China.

The decisions of the Ministry of Defence were taken by the Defence Acquisition Council, chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. These are two very important decisions which I'll bring you. First is a counter-UAV system for the Indian Army. This counter-UAV system will be based on an electronic warfare system, means that the this electronic warfare counter-UAV system will disable enemy drones trying to fly in or enemy small quadcopters or the drones which will be carrying small amount of payload. So this will be a kind of a disabler. This will be in addition to the guns, anti-drone guns and anti-drone weapons which are existing in the arsenal of the Indian Army. The second decision is about a high-altitude pseudo satellite. This will be for the Air Force. This pseudo satellite is actually like a plane. It has got fixed wings, it flies in the air, takes off from a runway and remain geostationary at a particular spot for a few weeks. It is powered by solar panels which are on the wings of the HAPS or the HAPS as it's being called by the military. These solar panels power the power this pseudo satellite for months. The third part of the DAC today, I beg your pardon, was about jet based Kamikaze drones. Now these jet based Kamikaze drones means there will be normal Kamikaze drones which will be powered by a jet engine. A Kamikaze drone is a drone which goes at a target and self-destructs. Kamikaze is a World War II word used by the Japanese forces for suicidal pilots in other words. So Kamikaze drone will go and hit the target and destroy itself. It is like a flying bomb or a missile. As Operation Sindoor has taught us and the standoff with China taught us during 20 to 2024. This story will keep on updating with me is tribune photographer Manas Ranjan Bhoy.

Rifleman Sunil Kumar received the Vir Chakra posthumously, and Sergeant Surendra Kumar the Vayu Sena Medal. This memorial lists soldiers who made the supreme sacrifice for the country after independence. Now, the six martyrs of Operation Sindoor are also part of this glorious list.

The six soldiers martyred in Operation Sindoor are:
1.  **Lance Naik Dinesh Kumar (Haryana):** 5 Field Regiment. Martyred on May 7, 2025, in Poonch sector responding to Pakistani shelling. His wife was pregnant.

4.  **Subedar Major Pawan Kumar (Himachal Pradesh):** Headquarters 10 Infantry Brigade. Chose a border posting despite nearing retirement. Succumbed to injuries on May 10, 2025, after Pakistani firing in Rajouri sector.
5.  **Rifleman Sunil Kumar (Jammu):** 4 Jammu and Kashmir Light Infantry. Did not leave his post and engaged the enemy in close combat. Posthumously awarded Vir Chakra.
6.  **Havaldar Sunil Kumar Singh (Bihar):** 237 Field Workshop Company. Alerted forces about Pakistani drone activity. Remained at post despite serious injuries. Posthumously awarded Sena Medal. Martyred on June 6, 2025.
